name: Emugrobart
lead: Emugrobart (GYM329, also RG6237 and RO7204239) is an injectable antibody developed by Chugai Pharmaceutical, majority-owned by Roche, that targets the latent form of myostatin, a protein that limits muscle growth [1]. It was designed to promote muscle and strength, and it was tested as a way to preserve or add muscle in people losing weight on GLP-1 and GIP drugs [2]. It is an investigational medicine available only in clinical trials; appearance-focused interest in it centres on the muscle-retention goal.

That body-composition angle is why it draws interest: weight-loss drugs reduce fat but can also reduce lean mass, and an anti-myostatin antibody aims to support muscle at the same time. Chugai's early research reported larger grip-strength gains in mouse models than other anti-myostatin agents, and increased muscle area on MRI in monkeys [1].
In 2026 Roche ended development in spinal muscular atrophy, facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy and obesity. Chugai has said it intends to continue the SMA program and seek partners [2][3].

chain: Muscle mass and strength supported, including during weight loss
angle.text: Emugrobart is an anti-myostatin antibody investigated to build or preserve muscle, notably alongside weight-loss drugs. It is a clinical-stage medicine, not something sold to consumers.

paras: Emugrobart was studied in three settings: spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) and overweight or obesity treated with incretin drugs [2][3]. The obesity program is the one most relevant to appearance, because it aimed to keep or increase lean mass while body fat falls.

The body-composition rationale reflects wider interest in myostatin, the signal that limits muscle size. Wikipedia reports that mice lacking the myostatin gene have about twice the normal muscle mass, that Belgian Blue cattle and some whippets carry mutations producing more muscle, and that a German boy with mutations in both gene copies was reported to be unusually strong [6]. Athletes seeking such drugs, according to the same article, have turned to the internet where products sold as 'myostatin blockers' circulate, and the World Anti-Doping Agency bans myostatin inhibitors [6].

The antibody binds latent (inactive) and precursor forms of myostatin and stops them from being activated; it does not bind mature myostatin or the related protein GDF11 [1]. It uses a sweeping design: an engineered Fc region lets the antibody-antigen complex enter cells through the FcgammaRIIb receptor, myostatin is released in the acidic endosome, and the antibody is recycled, which lowers myostatin levels in muscle and plasma [1].

Chugai's 2021 Scientific Reports paper describes GYM329 as a 'sweeping' antibody with an Fc region engineered for stronger binding to FcgammaRIIb and a Fab whose binding to myostatin depends on pH. The immune complex is taken into cells, the antigen is released in the acidic endosome and degraded, and the antibody is recycled through FcRn. A non-sweeping variant with the same in-vitro potency produced smaller strength gains in mice, even at a higher dose, and only the sweeping antibody lowered mature myostatin in muscle tissue and total myostatin in plasma [1].

Myostatin itself signals through the activin type II receptor to activate SMAD2 and SMAD3, which in mature muscle suppresses Akt-driven protein synthesis and promotes protein breakdown, according to Wikipedia [6]. Emugrobart acts earlier, by blocking activation of the latent precursor [1].

A Phase II FSHD study, MANOEUVRE (NCT05548556), enrolled adults aged 18 to 65. Roche reported that the drug was well tolerated, with no serious adverse events or withdrawals, but did not consistently improve muscle growth and motor function versus placebo, and it did not advance it to Phase III [3].

In obesity, the Phase II GYMINDA study tested emugrobart on top of tirzepatide for a 48-week core period [2]. On 28 September 2026, Chugai said Roche would stop clinical development of the subcutaneous anti-latent myostatin sweeping antibody for obesity after a data review, including an interim analysis of GYMINDA, concluded that the pre-specified goal of clinically meaningful weight loss was unlikely to be met. All rights licensed to Roche returned to Chugai, which began evaluating emugrobart for spinal muscular atrophy and said it was considering out-licensing the drug [2][7].
A 2026 review of myostatin inhibition in SMA discusses preclinical and clinical data for muscle-targeted therapies as a complement to treatments that raise SMN protein [4].

In the 2021 Scientific Reports paper from Chugai, whose authors are company employees, a mouse surrogate of the antibody was tested in a Duchenne model (mdx mice), in 79-week-old mice and in hindlimb-suspension atrophy, against landogrozumab and domagrozumab (anti-mature myostatin) and bimagrumab (anti-activin receptor). High doses of all agents gave similar muscle gains in the Duchenne model; in aged mice only the GYM329 surrogate and bimagrumab restored muscle mass to near-young levels; and in the atrophy model the GYM329 surrogate, domagrozumab and bimagrumab prevented muscle loss while landogrozumab did not [1].

On grip strength, the GYM329 surrogate gave the most consistent gains and was the only agent to significantly improve strength in aged and atrophy models, including at a lower dose in aged mice [1]. In cynomolgus monkeys (ten per dose group), a surrogate given intravenously every four weeks for two months increased muscle area on MRI and body weight versus vehicle and rapidly lowered plasma total myostatin; muscle function was not measured, all doses were described as well tolerated, and the authors called the safety data preliminary [1]. In the atrophy model, adding an anti-GDF11 antibody reduced the strength benefit, which the authors took to mean that GDF11 blockade works against strength gains [1].

The drug's development was reported in pharma-industry and patient-community outlets rather than consumer media. Pharmaphorum framed Roche's 2026 decision as the removal of a myostatin candidate from its obesity pipeline [2], the FSHD Society published Roche's letter to its community [3], and market reports noted share price declines for Chugai and Roche after the obesity announcement [7].

Interest in myostatin inhibitors in physique communities pre-dates emugrobart; other myostatin-pathway agents, including a Wyeth antibody (stamulumab) that is no longer in development and the activin/myostatin inhibitor ACE-031, were tested in early human studies, according to Wikipedia, and no myostatin-inhibiting drug had been approved for humans as of that article's 2012 account [6].

timeline.event: Myostatin gene identified by Se-Jin Lee and Alexandra McPherron; knockout mice show about twice normal muscle mass [6].
Chugai publishes preclinical data on GYM329 in mice and monkeys [1].
Roche ends development in SMA and FSHD after Phase II data [3].
Roche drops the obesity program and returns rights to Chugai; Chugai plans to continue SMA [2].
28 September: Chugai announces Roche will discontinue emugrobart in obesity after interim GYMINDA analysis; rights return to Chugai [7].

card.summary: An anti-myostatin antibody from Chugai/Roche tested to build or preserve muscle, including alongside weight-loss drugs.
card.note: Investigational only; Roche ended development in FSHD, SMA and obesity in 2026.

quick.overview:
Emugrobart is an antibody given by injection that binds latent myostatin, a brake on muscle growth. It was developed by Chugai, part of the Roche group, to support muscle in muscle-wasting diseases and in people losing weight on drugs such as tirzepatide.

Phase II trials in FSHD and obesity did not meet the hoped-for results, and Roche has ended its involvement. Chugai says it will keep exploring SMA.
quick.mechanism: The antibody captures latent myostatin and carries it into cells, where it is released and the antibody is recycled. This reduces myostatin in plasma and muscle, so less signalling restrains muscle growth.
quick.risks: In the FSHD trial it was well tolerated with no serious adverse events reported. It is investigational, not approved and not available outside trials.
